message.content: what I'm wondering mostly: this is an open data platform by the EU, so why publish data that you then can not use

content.text:
It isn't a paradox once you separate two things that both got called "publishing" — and our own evidence trail shows the mechanism.

**The mandate is transparency, not licensing.** Regulation (EU) 543/2013 obliges the industry to *expose* this data so market participants can see prices and flows, spot abuse, and trade informed, and so regulators can supervise. That duty is discharged by making it visible and accessible. It says nothing about granting downstream redistribution rights — and publishing something doesn't extinguish rights in it. Those are two separate legal layers stacked on the same numbers.

**ENTSO-E can only license what its members handed it rights to.** It's not an EU body — it's an AISBL, a Belgian non-profit association of transmission operators. Its terms speak of the "Primary Owner of Data," and that owner differs by item:

- Items on the free-re-use list — load forecasts, cross-zonal capacity, allocations, physical flows, redispatch, balancing — are **TSO-owned**. The TSOs collectively agreed to release their own data under CC BY 4.0 (that's the 2019 open-data move, with CC BY 4.0 folded into the list by amendment in 2022).
- The `12.1.d/e/f` block — energy prices, net positions, scheduled commercial exchanges — is **market results**, owned by the power exchanges/NEMOs: EPEX SPOT, Nord Pool and friends. Regulation compels them to feed it to the platform for transparency. It doesn't make them license it for republication — and selling market data is a substantial part of their commercial model.

So the list stops at `12.1.c` and resumes at `12.1.g` precisely along the ownership seam. ENTSO-E couldn't grant CC BY 4.0 over the middle block even if it wanted to.

**We already had independent confirmation of this and didn't recognise it.** energy-charts' own `/price` docs say the non-SMARD zones are "for private and internal use only" and direct licensing enquiries to "the original data providers, including but not limited to **EPEX SPOT SE**." That's the exchange asserting rights over exactly the series ENTSO-E can't sub-license. The list's other exclusions follow the same "who actually agreed" logic rather than anything technical: BritNed, IFA and Nemo Link are UK interconnectors, outside the regulation post-Brexit; Moldova and Turkey are non-EU parties.

**Why the German copy *is* open.** SMARD is run by the Bundesnetzagentur — a public authority, subject to public-sector open-data rules in a way an industry association isn't. It has its own legal basis to publish DE-LU and neighbouring-zone day-ahead prices, and chose CC BY 4.0. Same numbers, different publisher, genuinely different licence. That's why energy-charts can redistribute them "without changes," and why our original stack was licence-clean somewhat by luck.

**One European wrinkle worth knowing:** "it's just numbers, facts aren't copyrightable" is a much weaker argument here than in the US. The EU has a *sui generis* database right protecting substantial investment in compiling a database, so re-utilising a substantial part can be restricted even where no individual figure is. That's the hook that makes this more than a formality on this side of the Atlantic.

**The practical shape of it:** nothing stops you using ENTSO-E data for analysis, however deep — that's what the platform is *for*, and it's why the CLI on ENTSO-E is completely fine. **Redistribution is the constrained act**, and a public dashboard is redistribution. Since SMARD gives you the identical prices under CC BY 4.0, the fix isn't to give up data quality in general — it's to source the *published* page's prices from the publisher that licensed them.

Which is why I'd still revert the dashboard's data to energy-charts and keep ENTSO-E as the CLI default. The cost is confined to the public page's gross volumes and the DK_2 split; the headline balance, congestion rent and daily series are net-only and measured identical to 0.1 kEUR in 265 million. Want me to do that? It's one rebuild plus reverting `build_data.py`'s default — and the footer will switch its attribution back on its own.

content.text:
You got it the wrong way round, and I caused the confusion by quoting that warning twice as evidence for the ownership argument without restating who it applies to.

**All 12 zones this project queries are on energy-charts' CC BY 4.0 list** — verified above against the endpoint's own documented list, not from memory. DE-LU plus all 11 neighbours: AT, BE, CH, CZ, DK1, DK2, FR, NL, NO2, PL, SE4. Every one covered.

The "private and internal use only" restriction applies to **the other bidding zones** — ES, NO1, SE1–3, IT-South, GR and so on. Zones we never touch. The list also covers four we don't use (DE-AT-LU, HU, IT-North, SI), so there's headroom before the fence matters.

It's a fence around territory we deliberately stay inside, and `de_trade_balance.py`'s docstring already says exactly this: *"Prices for DE-LU and every zone bordering it are redistributed from SMARD under CC BY 4.0, so this use is fine. Other bidding zones on the same endpoint are marked private/internal use only — don't widen the border list and then publish the numbers."* That warning was written for the case where someone adds ES or NO1 to `NEIGHBOURS` and publishes — which would be a genuine problem.

So the two routes are not symmetrically constrained:

| | prices | cross-border flows |
|---|---|---|
| **energy-charts** | CC BY 4.0 from SMARD, all 12 zones we use, "published without changes" | no per-endpoint notice, so the API's blanket CC BY 4.0 default applies, with credit to Energy-Charts.info |
| **ENTSO-E** | `12.1.d` — **not** on the free-re-use list | `12.1.f` scheduled — **not** on the list; `12.1.g` physical — **is** on it |

The reason they differ is the mechanism from my last message: SMARD is a public authority that licensed these prices openly, so energy-charts gets to pass them along. ENTSO-E holds the same numbers from the exchanges under terms that don't permit onward licensing.

One honest caveat on the energy-charts column: `/cbet` carries no licence sentence of its own, so it rests on the API's general "unless stated otherwise, CC BY 4.0" — an inherited default rather than an explicit grant for that series. That's weaker than the prices, where the grant is spelled out zone by zone. If you want it airtight, a one-line email to Fraunhofer confirming `/cbet` is CC BY 4.0 would close it, and they're the same people who publish the CC BY 4.0 statement for `/price`.

So my recommendation stands and is better-founded than when I made it: revert the published dashboard to energy-charts, keep ENTSO-E for the CLI. Want me to run that?

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
build_data.py -- fetch a date range and merge it into the JSON the dashboard reads.

Everything analytical lives in de_trade_balance.py; this only reshapes its output
into one record per day and upserts it into docs/data/daily.json, so a daily cron
and a one-off backfill are the same code path.

    export ENTSOE_API_TOKEN=...              # the default source needs it
    ./build_data.py                          # yesterday, into docs/data/daily.json
    ./build_data.py --date 2026-07           # all of July
    ./build_data.py --date 2026-07-17 --days 31
    ./build_data.py --source energy-charts   # no token, netted flows

Upsert is by date, so re-running a day overwrites it in place -- which is what you
want, because both sources revise the last few days after first publication. Add
--refresh to overwrite days already on file that came from another source.

ENTSO-E is the default because it publishes each direction of a border separately.
The netted alternative agrees on balance_at_de_price to 0.0002% and on
congestion_rent to 0.6% -- both are net-only per MTU, so netting cannot move them
-- but its gross columns (import_gwh, export_gwh, and the volume-weighted prices
derived from them) run ~26% low, and it does not carry DK_2 at all. Each record
keeps the source it came from, and the dashboard credits and caveats per source.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
import os
import sys

import pandas as pd

import de_trade_balance as dtb

HERE = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
OUT = os.path.join(HERE, "docs", "data", "daily.json")
SCHEMA = 1


def _n(v, digits=2):
    """JSON-safe number: NaN/inf become null, everything else rounds."""
    if v is None or not pd.notna(v):
        return None
    return round(float(v), digits)


def day_records(d: pd.DataFrame, source: str, flows: str) -> list[dict]:
    """One record per calendar day, with its per-border breakdown nested."""
    day = dtb.per_period(d, "day")
    per_bd = dtb.per_border_period(d, "day")

    # the day's mean day-ahead price, deduplicated across borders first
    px = dtb._across_borders(d)["price_de"]
    px = px.groupby(dtb.period_of(px.index, "day")).mean()

    out = []
    for date, r in day.iterrows():
        borders = {}
        if date in per_bd.index.get_level_values("day"):
            for border, b in per_bd.xs(date, level="day").iterrows():
                borders[border] = {
                    "import_gwh": _n(b["import_GWh"]),
                    "export_gwh": _n(b["export_GWh"]),
                    "net_import_gwh": _n(b["net_imp_GWh"]),

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
build_data.py -- fetch a date range and merge it into the JSON the dashboard reads.

Everything analytical lives in de_trade_balance.py; this only reshapes its output
into one record per day and upserts it into docs/data/daily.json, so a daily cron
and a one-off backfill are the same code path.

    ./build_data.py                          # yesterday, into docs/data/daily.json
    ./build_data.py --date 2026-07           # all of July
    ./build_data.py --date 2026-07-17 --days 31
    ./build_data.py --source entsoe          # better data, but see the warning below

Upsert is by date, so re-running a day overwrites it in place -- which is what you
want, because both sources revise the last few days after first publication. It
also means switching source rewrites those days, so the dashboard's attribution
follows along on its own.


WHY THE DEFAULT IS energy-charts, AND WHY THAT IS NOT A DATA-QUALITY CALL
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
ENTSO-E is the better data: gross per-direction flows, and DK_2 present instead of
folded into DK_1. Use it freely for analysis -- that is what the CLI defaults to.

But this script feeds a *published* page, and publishing is redistribution, which
is a licensing question rather than a data one. ENTSO-E's list of data available
for free re-use (Article 2.5 of its terms) covers physical flows, 12.1.g, and does
not cover day-ahead prices, 12.1.d, or scheduled commercial exchanges, 12.1.f --
the whole 12.1.d/e/f market-results block is absent, because those belong to the
power exchanges rather than the TSOs, and ENTSO-E cannot sub-license what it does
not hold. energy-charts carries the same prices for DE-LU and all 11 neighbouring
zones under CC BY 4.0 from Bundesnetzagentur | SMARD.de, a public authority that
did license them openly.

So: --source entsoe to analyse, the default to publish. If you switch the site to
ENTSO-E for the gross volumes, you are making a licensing decision, not just a
data one. (Checked against the 18 Oct 2023 revision of that list; it does get

name: Daily balance

# Refreshes docs/data/daily.json and commits it. Pages serves docs/ straight from
# the branch, so the commit *is* the deploy -- there is nothing to publish here.
#
# Two things to know about the schedule:
#   * GitHub only fires `schedule` on the repository's DEFAULT branch. While this
#     lives on a side branch, the cron never runs; use workflow_dispatch, or make
#     this the default branch / merge it.
#   * It re-fetches the last few days rather than only yesterday, because both
#     sources revise recent days after first publication. Upsert is by date, so
#     re-fetching corrects a day in place instead of duplicating it.

on:
  schedule:
    - cron: "0 6 * * *"        # 06:00 UTC, comfortably after D-1 is settled
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      date:
        description: "Start: YYYY-MM-DD, YYYY-MM or YYYY (blank = last 3 days)"
        required: false
      end:
        description: "End, inclusive (optional)"
        required: false

permissions:
  contents: write

concurrency:
  group: daily-balance         # never let two runs race on the same file
  cancel-in-progress: false

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"

      - run: pip install --quiet pandas requests entsoe-py

      - name: Fetch and merge
        # Inputs arrive as env vars, never interpolated into the script body --
        # `${{ inputs.date }}` inline would be a shell-injection hole.
        env:
          IN_DATE: ${{ inputs.date }}
          IN_END: ${{ inputs.end }}
          # Settings -> Secrets and variables -> Actions -> ENTSOE_API_TOKEN.
          # Without it the job fails loudly rather than quietly falling back to a
          # source with different gross volumes, which would make the series a
          # mix of two definitions.
          ENTSOE_API_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.ENTSOE_API_TOKEN }}
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          if [ -z "${ENTSOE_API_TOKEN:-}" ]; then
            echo "::error::ENTSOE_API_TOKEN secret is not set. Add it, or pass" \
                 "--source energy-charts to build without a token."
            exit 1
          fi
          if [ -n "$IN_DATE" ]; then
            if [ -n "$IN_END" ]; then
              python3 build_data.py --date "$IN_DATE" --end "$IN_END"
            else
              python3 build_data.py --date "$IN_DATE"
            fi
          else
            python3 build_data.py \
              --date "$(date -u -d '3 days ago' +%F)" \
              --end  "$(date -u -d 'yesterday' +%F)"
          fi

      - name: Commit if the data moved
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          git config user.name  "github-actions[bot]"
          git config user.email "41898282+github-actions[bot]@users.noreply.github.com"
          git add docs/data/daily.json
          if git diff --staged --quiet; then
            echo "no change"
          else
            git commit -m "data: refresh through $(date -u +%F)"
            git push
          fi

toolUseResult.originalFile:
# German cross-border electricity balance

Did Germany pay more for imported electricity than it earned from exports? This
values every cross-border flow at day-ahead prices, per border and per market
time unit, and reports it over a day or a range.

```
de_trade_balance.py    the analysis and CLI report
build_data.py          reshapes a range into docs/data/daily.json
docs/                  the dashboard GitHub Pages serves
```

## Quick start

```bash
pip install pandas requests           # entsoe-py too, for --source entsoe
./de_trade_balance.py --date 2026-08-16          # one day, per MTU
./de_trade_balance.py --date 2026-07             # all of July, per day
./de_trade_balance.py --date 2026 --by week      # the year, per ISO week
./de_trade_balance.py --demo                     # synthetic, no network
```

No account needed: it defaults to Fraunhofer ISE's energy-charts API. Every raw
response is cached under `~/.cache/de_trade_balance`, which matters because that
API is rate limited per IP and endpoint and has no bulk export — a cold month of
all 11 borders costs ~90s and about a dozen requests, then it is free forever.

## The dashboard

```bash
python3 build_data.py --date 2026-07-18 --days 30   # fill the data file
cd docs && python3 -m http.server 8731              # then open localhost:8731
```

`build_data.py` upserts by date, so re-running a day corrects it in place. Both
sources revise the last few days after first publication, which is why the daily
job re-fetches a short trailing window rather than only yesterday.

### Publishing it

Settings → Pages → Source: **Deploy from a branch**, branch `site-daily-dashboard`,
folder **`/docs`**. The data file is committed, so each data commit is a deploy;
there is no build step and no CDN — the page is one HTML file with inline SVG
charts and no dependencies.

`.github/workflows/daily.yml` refreshes the data every morning and commits it.
**GitHub only fires `schedule` on the default branch**, so while this sits on a
side branch the cron will not run — trigger it by hand from the Actions tab
(`workflow_dispatch`, optionally with a date range to backfill), or merge this
branch to make the cron live.

## Which source to use

The dashboard is built from **ENTSO-E** (`build_data.py` defaults to it), because
it publishes each direction of a border separately and carries every bidding zone.
It needs a free token in `ENTSOE_API_TOKEN` and `pip install entsoe-py`; for the
daily job the token goes in Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions.

`de_trade_balance.py` still defaults to energy-charts, so the CLI and `--demo`
keep working with no account at all. Both scripts take `--source`.

Measured over July 2026, the two agree on `balance_at_de_price` to **0.0002%** and
on `congestion_rent` to 0.6% — not luck, but because both reduce to net-only
expressions per MTU:

```
balance_at_de_price = sum(net_MWh * price_de)
congestion_rent     = sum(net_MWh * spread)
```

so a source that reports flows already netted cannot shift either. What it does
shift is everything gross: energy-charts nets opposite flows within a border-hour,
so `import_gwh`/`export_gwh` come out ~26% low, and the volume-weighted prices are
biased apart. It also does not carry DK_2 — though the Kontek energy is still
there, filed under DK_1, so only the zonal pricing suffers.

## Reading the numbers

There is no single true figure, so three are reported. Cross-border trade in the
coupled day-ahead market is *implicit*: nobody buys a labelled MWh from France.
German buyers pay the German price, the seller abroad receives theirs, and the
difference is congestion rent collected by the transmission operators on both
sides — regulated back into grid fees and interconnector investment, not a loss.

Day-ahead only: intraday and balancing trades settle at other prices and are not
included. The long-form version of all of this is the docstring at the top of
`de_trade_balance.py`.

## Attribution

Day-ahead prices for Germany and its neighbours are
[CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/) from
[Bundesnetzagentur | SMARD.de](https://www.smard.de), redistributed unchanged by
[Energy-Charts.info](https://www.energy-charts.info) (Fraunhofer ISE), which is
also the source of the cross-border exchange series. Other bidding zones on that
endpoint are marked private/internal use only — don't widen the border list and
then publish the numbers.

Done — committed as `6990abd`. Refresh **http://localhost:8731** and it's back on the licence-clean source.

**Verified on the live page:** provenance reads `via energy-charts`, the footer is back to the SMARD CC BY 4.0 credit, the netting caveat has returned to the Volumes card, 10 border rows, no console errors.

**What the switch cost, measured:**

```
                       entsoe   energy-charts
balance kEUR       -265,314.4      -265,314.3     ← 0.1 kEUR apart
rent kEUR           107,230.3       107,247.6     ← 0.02%
net GWh                  18.1            18.1     ← identical
imported GWh          5,290.7         3,850.5     ← the real cost, 27% low
```

Everything the page leads with is untouched, because those quantities are net-only per MTU. The loss is confined to gross volumes and the DK_2 split — both flagged in the UI rather than hidden.

**Three places now carry the reasoning**, because "ENTSO-E is better data" is true and someone (including future me) will be tempted to switch back without knowing the constraint:

- `build_data.py` — a docstring section headed "why the default is energy-charts, and why that is not a data-quality call"
- `.github/workflows/daily.yml` — a comment at the fetch step, noting it's deliberately not configurable there
- `README.md` — the article-by-article table plus the ownership explanation

**Two loose ends worth your attention:**

- The daily job no longer needs `ENTSOE_API_TOKEN` as a repo secret. If you already added it, it's now unused — harmless, but you may prefer to remove it.
- `/cbet` still rests on energy-charts' blanket "unless stated otherwise, CC BY 4.0" rather than an explicit per-series grant, unlike the prices. That's the one soft spot in the chain. A one-line email to Fraunhofer would close it, if you want it airtight before publishing.

And the finding that started this: your instinct that an EU transparency platform ought to be usable was right about the *intent* — the mandate genuinely does make this data open to look at and analyse. It just doesn't carry redistribution rights for the market-results block, because those aren't the TSOs' to give. Your original stack was already the correct one for publishing; we just now know *why*, rather than by luck.

content.text:
Your second instinct is exactly right, and it's the whole answer: **buying in DK isn't a separate transaction that happens after the auction — it's part of how the price was reached.** Let me build up to that, because the data backs it precisely.

## First, a correction on "highest bidder"

It's *marginal* pricing, not highest-bidder. All supply offers get sorted cheapest-first, demand bids most-expensive-first, and they cross. Everyone who clears pays (or receives) the **same** price — the one set by the last, most expensive offer that was still needed. Bids above the crossing don't clear at all.

So German wind isn't outcompeted by Danish wind. Wind bids near zero and always clears; it just receives whatever the marginal plant set. What imports displace is the **marginal** unit — the last gas or hard-coal plant needed to close the gap.

That reverses the direction of your hypothesis in an important way: **imports don't make the night price high — they make it less high.** At 20:00 the price was €173.7 because solar was gone and demand needed expensive plants. The 8,507 MW flowing in pushed the most expensive German units out of the stack. Without that import the German price would have been *higher*.

## Why there's flow at all, when the market "already cleared"

There is no German auction plus a Danish auction plus trade between them. There is **one** algorithm (SDAC, running EUPHEMIA) clearing every bidding zone simultaneously, with interconnector capacities as constraints, maximising total welfare across the whole coupled area. Prices and flows are computed *together*, in one solve. The flow is an output, not a decision anyone makes afterwards.

Nobody "buys from Denmark." German buyers bid into the German zone and pay the German price. The algorithm has already routed Danish supply in, because doing so raised welfare. So yes — it's part of the same clearing price, precisely as you guessed.

Then why do the zones have *different* prices?

- **Cable has slack** → the algorithm keeps pushing power from cheap to dear until the two prices **equalise**. One price, no rent.
- **Cable saturates** → it can't push more, so prices stay apart. That gap × the flow is the congestion rent.

Our data says the cables bind almost all the time: prices fully converged in only **0–12% of hours** per border (NL best at 12.0%, CH and NO2 at 0.1%). That's why Europe has 11 prices instead of one.

## The profile is textbook

```
hour   price €/MWh    net flow
04         128.5      +5,416 MW  importing
06         141.5      +6,948 MW  importing
14          19.5      -8,816 MW  exporting   ← solar peak
20         173.7      +5,094 MW  importing   ← evening peak
```

Correlation between the German hourly price and net import: **+0.82**. Germany imports when expensive, exports when cheap, and the driver is its own solar profile — the price bottoms at 14:00 (€19.5) and peaks at 21:00 (€174.1).

And the flows follow the spread, as arbitrage requires:

- Imports came from a **cheaper** zone for **73.3%** of imported MWh (9.1% converged, 17.6% dearer)
- Exports went to a **dearer** zone for **81.3%** of exported MWh

The 17.6% "wrong way" isn't market irrationality. Partly it's our known artifacts — unsplit Denmark, netted flows hiding simultaneous two-way movement, hourly averaging over 15-minute clearing, and scheduled exchanges including intraday volume that a day-ahead price doesn't govern. But partly it's genuine: the Core region uses **flow-based** coupling, where capacity is a joint domain across many borders rather than a limit per cable, so an individual border can legitimately carry power "uphill" while the overall solution is optimal.

## The part that matters for reading your own dashboard

This profile is exactly why **the −€265M is not a loss**, and why the headline is the most easily misread number on the page.

Germany imports in expensive hours because that's when it's short — and those imports *lower* the price its consumers pay. It exports in cheap hours because it's long — and those exports earn its generators money that curtailed solar would not have. Every one of those trades improved both sides; that's why the algorithm selected them. Without the interconnectors, German peak prices would be higher and midday solar would be spilled instead of sold.

What the −€265M actually measures is a **valuation asymmetry**: net import correlates with high prices at +0.82, so the same MWh count is worth more coming in than going out. That's a fact about *when* Germany trades, not evidence that anyone extracted value from it. Which is why the timing term dominated (90% of July) while net volume was a rounding error (18 GWh on 5,291).

One nice sighting in the border table: **SE4 shows a persistent +€27/MWh spread with zero flow all month.** If the cable were available, the algorithm would have arbitraged that instantly — you cannot leave €27/MWh on the table in a coupled market. Zero flow against a standing spread means the interconnector was simply out. The mechanism showing itself by its absence.

content.text:
No — and the concept doesn't quite exist in this market design either.

**What we actually get.** `/price` returns exactly this per zone:

```
{"license_info": str, "unix_seconds": [int], "price": [float], "unit": str, "deprecated": bool}
```

One number per market time unit. No technology dimension, and **no bid or order-book endpoint exists on the API at all** — I checked every path for bid/curve/merit/order/offer.

**The deeper reason it can't.** In a uniform-price auction there is no price *per* technology. Everything that clears receives the same price. What differs is:

- what a plant would **bid** — roughly its marginal cost: fuel + CO₂ + variable O&M; near zero, or negative under subsidy, for wind and solar
- what it **receives** — the single clearing price

The gap between those is inframarginal rent, and it's how a wind farm bidding €0 earns €174 at 21:00. So "the price of wind" isn't a published figure; it's the clearing price, same as everyone else's. The only technology-linked price in the system is the **marginal** unit's cost, because that's what sets the clearing price for all of them.

**Where bid-level data does and doesn't live:**

- **Day-ahead aggregated supply/demand curves** — the actual merit-order curves — are published by the exchanges (EPEX SPOT, Nord Pool) for their own markets. Commercially licensed, not on ENTSO-E's platform, not on energy-charts. Exactly the ownership pattern from our licence dig: market microstructure is exchange property.
- **Balancing** bids *are* public: aggregated balancing energy bids sit on ENTSO-E's free-re-use list as item #26 (articles 17.1.d/e/j). So bid-level data exists for balancing, just not for day-ahead energy.
- **Generation per technology** is freely available on both sources — volumes, not prices.

**What you can do with what's licensed** is infer which technology was marginal, by joining the price series to the generation stack. energy-charts' `/public_power` returns 21 series for Germany:

```
lignite · hard coal · fossil gas · fossil oil · coal-derived gas · nuclear-free stack
wind onshore · wind offshore · solar · biomass · waste · geothermal
hydro run-of-river · reservoir · pumped storage (+ its consumption)
load · residual load · renewable share of load / of generation
```

Residual load is the useful one: load minus wind and solar is essentially "how deep into the thermal stack we had to reach," and it tracks price closely. That's how you'd get from our data to "gas set the price at 21:00, solar set it at 14:00" — an inference from volumes plus price, not a lookup.

It would also be **licence-clean**: no per-endpoint restriction on `/public_power`, so it falls under the same blanket CC BY 4.0, and SMARD publishes German generation per type openly too.

Worth adding to the dashboard? It would answer the question your current page raises but can't settle — *what* Germany was importing instead of, hour by hour. A residual-load or stack panel beside the price chart would close that loop. Say the word and I'll scope it.

content.text:
Yes — considerably more detail, and one finding **dissolves the trade-off I told you was unavoidable.**

## The big one: SMARD has gross per-direction cross-border flows

Separate Import *and* Export series per neighbour, with DK1 and DK2 as distinct borders. Cross-validated against ENTSO-E for 18 July:

```
                    SMARD    ENTSO-E   delta
DK_1 into DE       33,349     33,350      -1 MWh
DK_1 out of DE     36,968     36,970      -2
DK_2 into DE       11,939     11,940      -1
DK_2 out of DE      2,503      2,500      +3
```

Identical to rounding. So SMARD gives you **exactly what ENTSO-E gave** — gross volumes, no netting loss, DK_2 as its own border — from a **public authority publishing under CC BY 4.0**. You would not have to choose between correct gross volumes and a publishable licence. That was the whole cost of reverting, and it turns out to be avoidable.

It also puts the `/cbet` soft spot to rest: instead of resting on energy-charts' blanket "unless stated otherwise" default, the flows would carry the same explicit public-authority licence as the prices.

## What else is there

**More than energy-charts:**
- **Prices for 17 zones** — including SE4, Belgium and NO2, which definitively settles that the community `bund.dev` spec I first consulted was just incomplete
- **Installed capacity** per technology
- **Generation forecasts**, day-ahead *and* intraday
- **Residual load**, both realised and forecast — the "how deep into the thermal stack did we reach" series from your last question
- **Balancing energy**: volumes (+/−), **price**, revenues
- **System costs**: balancing expenditure, countertrading, grid-security measures (redispatch)
- **Per-TSO breakdown** — Amprion, TenneT, TransnetBW as separate control areas

**Less than energy-charts, in one respect:** generation is 12 types versus energy-charts' 21. SMARD lumps into "Sonstige Konventionelle"/"Sonstige Erneuerbare" where energy-charts (using ENTSO-E's taxonomy) breaks out fossil oil, coal-derived gas, geothermal, waste, and three hydro categories separately. So for a generation-mix panel, energy-charts is finer; for everything else, SMARD is deeper.

**Still no day-ahead bid curves** — that answers your previous question for SMARD too. `Ausgleichsenergiepreis` is a genuine auction-derived price, but for balancing, not the day-ahead merit order. The day-ahead curves really do stay with the exchanges.

## The API, since it isn't documented anywhere useful

I had to reverse it from the site's own network traffic:

```
manifest   /app/chart_configuration/market_data_configuration.json   (321 modules with IDs)
labels     /app/assets/translations/lang-de.json
regions    /app/chart_configuration/regions.json
download   POST /nip-download-manager/nip/download/market-data → CSV
```

Two gotchas worth recording: the region must be **`DE-LU`** for cross-border modules (`DE` returns "Keine Daten"), and the CSV is German-formatted with imports as **negative** numbers.

## Worth building?

A SMARD backend would give the dashboard ENTSO-E-quality volumes on a licence that permits publishing — strictly better than either source we've used. It's real work: mapping 11 borders × 2 directions to module IDs, German decimal parsing, sign conventions, and a chunking strategy against an undocumented endpoint. Maybe an evening.

Two smaller things it would also unlock: DK_2 finally appearing on the public page, and the residual-load series for the "what set the price" panel we discussed.

Want me to scope it properly, or build it? I'd verify the module mapping across all 11 borders and a few dates first — I've only proven Denmark on one day, and an undocumented manifest is exactly the kind of thing that has surprises in the tail.

attachment.snippet:
1	#!/usr/bin/env python3
2	"""
3	de_trade_balance.py -- Did Germany pay more for imported electricity than it
4	earned from exports, over a day or over a longer range?
5	
6	Pulls, per border and per market time unit (MTU):
7	  * cross-border exchange DE-LU <-> neighbour, both directions
8	  * day-ahead price of DE-LU and of the neighbouring bidding zone
9	
10	...then values the flows and prints a per-border summary plus a time series at
11	whatever resolution the range warrants (MTU, day, ISO week, month, year).
12	
13	Data source: ENTSO-E Transparency Platform (https://transparency.entsoe.eu).
14	Requires a free API token: register, then Account Settings -> "Generate a new
15	token" (older accounts: email transparency@entsoe.eu asking for API access).
16	
17	    export ENTSOE_API_TOKEN=...             # --source entsoe only
18	    pip install entsoe-py pandas requests
19	    ./de_trade_balance.py --date 2026-08-16                    # one day, per MTU
20	    ./de_trade_balance.py --date 2026-07                       # all of July, per day
21	    ./de_trade_balance.py --date 2026 --by week                # the year, ISO weeks
22	    ./de_trade_balance.py --date 2026-01-01 --end 2026-06-30 --by month
23	    ./de_trade_balance.py --date 2026-08-16 --flows physical --csv out/
24	    ./de_trade_balance.py --demo                               # synthetic data
25	
26	
27	A NOTE ON WHAT "COST" MEANS HERE
28	-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
29	There is no single true number, so this script reports three.
30	
31	In the coupled European day-ahead market, cross-border trade is *implicit*:
32	nobody buys a labelled MWh "from France". Buyers in a zone pay their own zonal
33	price, sellers in a zone receive their own zonal price, and the algorithm moves
34	power across a border until either the prices converge or the interconnector
35	saturates. So for one MWh flowing X -> DE:
36	
37	    German buyers pay          P_DE
38	    the seller in X receives   P_X
39	    the difference (P_DE-P_X)  is congestion rent, collected by the two TSOs
40	                               (normally split 50/50, and regulated back into
41	                               grid fees / interconnector investment)
42	
43	Hence:
44	
45	  balance_at_de_price   Everything valued at the German price. This is the
46	                        "what did this volume trade for at home" view and the
47	                        one journalism usually means. Under this metric, if DE
48	                        is a net importer in expensive hours and a net exporter
49	                        in cheap hours, the balance is negative.
50	
51	                        Worth seeing that it collapses to
52	                        sum(net_MWh * price_de) per MTU: both directions carry
53	                        the same price, so gross volumes cancel and only the
54	                        net position in each hour survives. That makes it the
55	                        sturdiest of the three -- indifferent to whether the
56	                        source reports flows gross or already netted -- and it
57	                        is also why it says nothing about how much trade
58	                        actually took place.
59	
60	  balance_at_zonal      Imports valued at the exporting zone's price, exports
61	                        valued at the German price -- i.e. money actually
62	                        leaving/entering the German market area, ignoring
63	                        congestion rent. Almost always the friendlier number.
64	
65	  congestion_rent       Rent on both legs, which works out as
66	                        sum(net_MWh * spread) per border and MTU: imports earn
67	                        it when P_DE > P_X, exports when P_X > P_DE. Not a loss;
68	                        it is revenue to the two TSOs on that border, normally
69	                        split 50/50.
70	
71	                        It is *not* the gap between the two balances above, easy
72	                        as that is to assume. balance_at_zonal only re-prices
73	                        the import leg -- exports sit at the German price in
74	                        both metrics -- so the gap is the import-side rent
75	                        alone: 43.6 of 99.6 MEUR over July 2026. The export-side
76	                        rent is real TSO revenue that neither balance reports.
77	
78	                        Being net-only per border, it is as indifferent to gross
79	                        volumes as balance_at_de_price. entsoe and energy-charts
80	                        agreed on it to 0.6% for July 2026 despite differing by
81	                        1,499 GWh of gross bidirectional flow; what little gap
82	                        remains is DK_2 finally being priced at its own zone.
83	
84	Also worth keeping in mind:
85	  * Day-ahead is the bulk of it, not all of it. Intraday and balancing trades
86	    are settled at other prices and are not included here.
87	  * "physical" flows (metered, includes loop and transit flows) differ from
88	    "scheduled" commercial exchanges. Only the latter has a price attached in
89	    any meaningful sense, so it is the default. Physical is available for
90	    comparison via --flows physical.
91	  * Luxembourg is inside the DE-LU bidding zone, so it is not a "border" here.
92	  * Austria was in the same zone as DE until 1 Oct 2018; dates before that
93	    need Area.DE_AT_LU and are not handled.
94	
95	
96	RANGES AND PERIOD AGGREGATION
97	-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
98	--date takes a day (2026-08-16), a month (2026-07) or a year (2026) and covers
99	exactly that span, unless --end (inclusive, same three forms) or --days says
100	otherwise. --by sets the resolution of the time-series table: mtu, day, week,
101	month, year, or auto -- the default, which picks one from the length of the
102	range. Per-border totals always cover the whole range regardless of --by.
103	
104	Weeks are ISO weeks (%G-W%V), so "2026-W01" is Mon 29 Dec 2025 to Sun 4 Jan
105	2026 and the label carries the ISO year, not the calendar one.
106

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
build_data.py -- fetch a date range and merge it into the JSON the dashboard reads.

Everything analytical lives in de_trade_balance.py; this only reshapes its output
into one record per day and upserts it into docs/data/daily.json, so a daily cron
and a one-off backfill are the same code path.

    ./build_data.py                          # yesterday, into docs/data/daily.json
    ./build_data.py --date 2026-07           # all of July
    ./build_data.py --date 2026-07-17 --days 31
    ./build_data.py --source entsoe          # better data, but see the warning below

Upsert is by date, so re-running a day overwrites it in place -- which is what you
want, because both sources revise the last few days after first publication. It
also means switching source rewrites those days, so the dashboard's attribution
follows along on its own.


WHY THE DEFAULT IS energy-charts, AND WHY THAT IS NOT A DATA-QUALITY CALL
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
ENTSO-E is the better data: gross per-direction flows, and DK_2 present instead of
folded into DK_1. Use it freely for analysis -- that is what the CLI defaults to.

But this script feeds a *published* page, and publishing is redistribution, which
is a licensing question rather than a data one. ENTSO-E's list of data available
for free re-use (Article 2.5 of its terms) covers physical flows, 12.1.g, and does
not cover day-ahead prices, 12.1.d, or scheduled commercial exchanges, 12.1.f --
the whole 12.1.d/e/f market-results block is absent, because those belong to the
power exchanges rather than the TSOs, and ENTSO-E cannot sub-license what it does
not hold. energy-charts carries the same prices for DE-LU and all 11 neighbouring
zones under CC BY 4.0 from Bundesnetzagentur | SMARD.de, a public authority that
did license them openly.

So: --source entsoe to analyse, the default to publish. If you switch the site to
ENTSO-E for the gross volumes, you are making a licensing decision, not just a
data one. (Checked against the 18 Oct 2023 revision of that list; it does get
amended, so it is worth re-reading before relying on this.)
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
import os
import sys

import pandas as pd

import de_trade_balance as dtb

HERE = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
OUT = os.path.join(HERE, "docs", "data", "daily.json")
SCHEMA = 1


def _n(v, digits=2):
    """JSON-safe number: NaN/inf become null, everything else rounds."""
    if v is None or not pd.notna(v):
        return None
    return round(float(v), digits)


def day_records(d: pd.DataFrame, source: str, flows: str) -> list[dict]:
    """One record per calendar day, with its per-border breakdown nested."""
    day = dtb.per_period(d, "day")
    per_bd = dtb.per_border_period(d, "day")

    # the day's mean day-ahead price, deduplicated across borders first
    px = dtb._across_borders(d)["price_de"]
    px = px.groupby(dtb.period_of(px.index, "day")).mean()

    out = []
    for date, r in day.iterrows():
        borders = {}
        if date in per_bd.index.get_level_values("day"):
            for border, b in per_bd.xs(date, level="day").iterrows():
                borders[border] = {
                    "import_gwh": _n(b["import_GWh"]),
                    "export_gwh": _n(b["export_GWh"]),
                    "net_import_gwh": _n(b["net_imp_GWh"]),
                    "bal_de_keur": _n(b["bal_de_kEUR"], 1),
                    "rent_keur": _n(b["rent_kEUR"], 1),
                    "mean_spread": _n(b["mean_spread"]),
                }
        out.append({
            "date": date,
            "source": source,
            "flows": flows,
            "price_de_mean": _n(px.get(date)),
            "import_gwh": _n(r["import_GWh"]),
            "export_gwh": _n(r["export_GWh"]),
            "net_import_gwh": _n(r["net_imp_GWh"]),
            "imp_px_de": _n(r["imp_px_de"]),
            "exp_px_de": _n(r["exp_px_de"]),
            "bal_de_keur": _n(r["bal_de_kEUR"], 1),
            "bal_zonal_keur": _n(r["bal_zonal_kEUR"], 1),
            "rent_keur": _n(r["rent_kEUR"], 1),
            "borders": borders,
        })
    return out


def merge(path: str, fresh: list[dict], borders_asked: list) -> dict:
    """Upsert by date into whatever is already on disk."""
    try:
        with open(path) as fh:
            store = json.load(fh)
    except (OSError, ValueError):
        store = {}

    by_date = {r["date"]: r for r in store.get("days", [])}
    added = sum(1 for r in fresh if r["date"] not in by_date)
    by_date.update({r["date"]: r for r in fresh})

    store["schema"] = SCHEMA
    store["generated_at"] = pd.Timestamp.now(tz=dtb.TZ).isoformat(timespec="seconds")
    store["timezone"] = dtb.TZ
    store["borders_requested"] = list(borders_asked)
    store["units"] = {"gwh": "GWh", "keur": "thousand EUR", "px": "EUR/MWh"}
    store["days"] = [by_date[k] for k in sorted(by_date)]
    print(f"  {added} new day(s), {len(fresh) - added} updated, "
          f"{len(store['days'])} total")
    return store


def write(path: str, store: dict) -> None:

1	#!/usr/bin/env python3
2	"""
3	build_data.py -- fetch a date range and merge it into the JSON the dashboard reads.
4	
5	Everything analytical lives in de_trade_balance.py; this only reshapes its output
6	into one record per day and upserts it into docs/data/daily.json, so a daily cron
7	and a one-off backfill are the same code path.
8	
9	    ./build_data.py                          # yesterday, into docs/data/daily.json
10	    ./build_data.py --date 2026-07           # all of July
11	    ./build_data.py --date 2026-07-17 --days 31
12	    ./build_data.py --source entsoe          # better data, but see the warning below
13	
14	Upsert is by date, so re-running a day overwrites it in place -- which is what you
15	want, because both sources revise the last few days after first publication. It
16	also means switching source rewrites those days, so the dashboard's attribution
17	follows along on its own.
18	
19	
20	WHY THE DEFAULT IS SMARD
21	-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
22	It is the only source that is both publishable and complete.
23	
24	The trade-off looked unavoidable for a while. ENTSO-E has the better shape --
25	gross per-direction flows, DK_2 as its own border -- but its list of data
26	available for free re-use (Article 2.5 of its terms) covers physical flows at
27	12.1.g and does *not* cover day-ahead prices at 12.1.d or scheduled commercial
28	exchanges at 12.1.f. The whole 12.1.d/e/f market-results block is absent, because
29	it belongs to the power exchanges rather than the TSOs, and ENTSO-E cannot
30	sub-license rights it does not hold. energy-charts is cleanly licensed but nets
31	opposite flows within each border-hour, so its gross volumes run ~27% low and
32	Denmark arrives unsplit.
33	
34	SMARD is both: Bundesnetzagentur is the primary publisher and a public authority,
35	its data is CC BY 4.0, and it carries each direction of each border separately.
36	Cross-checked against ENTSO-E for 2026-07-18 -- all 11 borders, both directions,
37	agreeing to under 0.02 GWh.
38	
39	So the ordering is: SMARD to publish, ENTSO-E to cross-check, energy-charts as the
40	no-fuss fallback. (The re-use list checked was the 18 Oct 2023 revision; it gets
41	amended, so re-read it before leaning on the ENTSO-E half of this.)
42	"""
43	
44	from __future__ import annotations
45	
46	import argparse
47	import json
48	import os
49	import sys
50	
51	import pandas as pd
52	
53	import de_trade_balance as dtb
54	
55	HERE = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
56	OUT = os.path.join(HERE, "docs", "data", "daily.json")
57	SCHEMA = 1
58	
59	
60	def _n(v, digits=2):
61	    """JSON-safe number: NaN/inf become null, everything else rounds."""
62	    if v is None or not pd.notna(v):
63	        return None
64	    return round(float(v), digits)
65	
66	
67	def demand_daily(backend, start, end) -> pd.DataFrame | None:
68	    """Daily mean load and residual load in GW, when the backend has them.
69	
70	    Residual load is load minus wind and solar -- how far into the dispatchable
71	    stack the day had to reach. It is the closest thing to an answer for "what set
72	    this price", which the balance itself cannot say.
73	    """
74	    if not hasattr(backend, "demand"):
75	        return None
76	    frames = []
77	    for ws, we in dtb.windows(start, end, "month"):
78	        try:
79	            frames.append(backend.demand(ws, we))
80	        except Exception as exc:
81	            print(f"  ! demand {ws.date()}: {type(exc).__name__}: {exc}", file=sys.stderr)
82	    if not frames:
83	        return None
84	    df = pd.concat(frames).sort_index()
85	    df = df[(df.index >= start) & (df.index < end)]
86	    g = df.groupby(dtb.period_of(df.index, "day"))
87	    return pd.DataFrame({"load_gw": g["load_mw"].mean() / 1000,
88	                         "residual_gw": g["residual_mw"].mean() / 1000})
89	
90	
91	def day_records(d: pd.DataFrame, source: str, flows: str,
92	                demand: pd.DataFrame | None = None) -> list[dict]:
93	    """One record per calendar day, with its per-border breakdown nested."""
94	    day = dtb.per_period(d, "day")
95	    per_bd = dtb.per_border_period(d, "day")
96	
97	    # the day's mean day-ahead price, deduplicated across borders first
98	    px = dtb._across_borders(d)["price_de"]
99	    px = px.groupby(dtb.period_of(px.index, "day")).mean()
100	
101	    out = []
102	    for date, r in day.iterrows():
103	        borders = {}
104	        if date in per_bd.index.get_level_values("day"):
105	            for border, b in per_bd.xs(date, level="day").iterrows():
106	                borders[border] = {
107	                    "import_gwh": _n(b["import_GWh"]),
108	                    "export_gwh": _n(b["export_GWh"]),
109	                    "net_import_gwh": _n(b["net_imp_GWh"]),
110	                    "bal_de_keur": _n(b["bal_de_kEUR"], 1),
111	                    "rent_keur": _n(b["rent_kEUR"], 1),
112	                    "mean_spread": _n(b["mean_spread"]),
113	                }
114	        dm = demand.loc[date] if demand is not None and date in demand.index else None
115	        out.append({
116	            "date": date,
117	            "source": source,
118	            "flows": flows,
119	            "price_de_mean": _n(px.get(date)),
120	            "load_gw": _n(dm["load_gw"]) if dm is not None else None,
121	            "residual_gw": _n(dm["residual_gw"]) if dm is not None else None,
122	            "import_gwh": _n(r["import_GWh"]),
123	            "export_gwh": _n(r["export_GWh"]),
124	            "net_import_gwh": _n(r["net_imp_GWh"]),
125	            "imp_px_de": _n(r["imp_px_de"]),
126	            "exp_px_de": _n(r["exp_px_de"]),
127	            "bal_de_keur": _n(r["bal_de_kEUR"], 1),
128	            "bal_zonal_keur": _n(r["bal_zonal_kEUR"], 1),
129	            "rent_keur": _n(r["rent_kEUR"], 1),
130	            "borders": borders,
131	        })
132	    return out
133	
134	
135	def merge(path: str, fresh: list[dict], borders_asked: list) -> dict:
136	    """Upsert by date into whatever is already on disk."""
137	    try:
138	        with open(path) as fh:
139	            store = json.load(fh)
140	    except (OSError, ValueError):
141	        store = {}
142	
143	    by_date = {r["date"]: r for r in store.get("days", [])}
144	    added = sum(1 for r in fresh if r["date"] not in by_date)
145	    by_date.update({r["date"]: r for r in fresh})
146	
147	    store["schema"] = SCHEMA
148	    store["generated_at"] = pd.Timestamp.now(tz=dtb.TZ).isoformat(timespec="seconds")
149	    store["timezone"] = dtb.TZ
150	    store["borders_requested"] = list(borders_asked)
151	    store["units"] = {"gwh": "GWh", "keur": "thousand EUR", "px": "EUR/MWh"}
152	    store["days"] = [by_date[k] for k in sorted(by_date)]
153	    print(f"  {added} new day(s), {len(fresh) - added} updated, "
154	          f"{len(store['days'])} total")
155	    return store
156	
157	
158	def write(path: str, store: dict) -> None:
159	    os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(path), exist_ok=True)
160	    tmp = f"{path}.tmp"
161	    with open(tmp, "w") as fh:
162	        json.dump(store, fh, indent=1, sort_keys=False)
163	        fh.write("\n")
164	    os.replace(tmp, path)

lines: +/** Residual load against price, one dot per day.
+ *  A scatter rather than two lines on one time axis: they are different measures
+ *  (GW and €/MWh), and putting both on a shared time axis would need two y-scales
+ *  -- the one chart form that reliably invents a correlation. Here each measure
+ *  owns an axis and the relationship is the thing you read. Dot colour carries the
+ *  day's trade direction, tying the mechanism back to the balance above.
+  const pts = days.filter(d => d.residual_gw != null && d.price_de_mean != null);
+  const H2 = 240, W = host.clientWidth || 720, H = H2 + PAD.t + PAD.b + 8;
+  const svg = el("svg", { viewBox: `0 0 ${W} ${H}`, width: W, height: H, role: "img",
+    "aria-label": "Daily mean day-ahead price against residual load" });
+  const x0 = PAD.l + 6, x1 = W - PAD.r, y0 = PAD.t + 8, y1 = PAD.t + 8 + H2;
+  const xs = pts.map(d => d.residual_gw), ys = pts.map(d => d.price_de_mean);
+  const x = scale(xlo - xp, xhi + xp, x0, x1), y = scale(ylo - yp, yhi + yp, y1, y0);
+  for (const t of ticks(ylo - yp, yhi + yp, 4)) {
+    svg.append(el("line", { class: "gridline", x1: x0, x2: x1, y1: y(t), y2: y(t) }));
+    svg.append(el("text", { class: "tick", x: x0 - 8, y: y(t) + 4, "text-anchor": "end" }, num(t)));
+  for (const t of ticks(xlo - xp, xhi + xp, 5)) {
+    svg.append(el("line", { class: "gridline", x1: x(t), x2: x(t), y1: y0, y2: y1 }));
+    svg.append(el("text", { class: "tick", x: x(t), y: y1 + 17, "text-anchor": "middle" }, num(t)));
+  svg.append(el("text", { x: x1, y: y1 + 30, "text-anchor": "end" }, "residual load, GW"));
+    svg.append(el("circle", { cx: x(d.residual_gw), cy: y(d.price_de_mean), r: 5,
+    // hit target well past the mark, so a 10px dot is still easy to catch
+    const hit = el("circle", { class: "hit", cx: x(d.residual_gw), cy: y(d.price_de_mean), r: 13 });
+  // Pearson r, so the hint states the strength instead of implying it
+  const mx = xs.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) / xs.length;
+  const my = ys.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) / ys.length;
+    const dx = xs[i] - mx, dy = ys[i] - my;
+    sxy += dx * dy; sxx += dx * dx; syy += dy * dy;

name: Daily balance

# Refreshes docs/data/daily.json and commits it. Pages serves docs/ straight from
# the branch, so the commit *is* the deploy -- there is nothing to publish here.
#
# Two things to know about the schedule:
#   * GitHub only fires `schedule` on the repository's DEFAULT branch. While this
#     lives on a side branch, the cron never runs; use workflow_dispatch, or make
#     this the default branch / merge it.
#   * It re-fetches the last few days rather than only yesterday, because both
#     sources revise recent days after first publication. Upsert is by date, so
#     re-fetching corrects a day in place instead of duplicating it.

on:
  schedule:
    - cron: "0 6 * * *"        # 06:00 UTC, comfortably after D-1 is settled
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      date:
        description: "Start: YYYY-MM-DD, YYYY-MM or YYYY (blank = last 3 days)"
        required: false
      end:
        description: "End, inclusive (optional)"
        required: false

permissions:
  contents: write

concurrency:
  group: daily-balance         # never let two runs race on the same file
  cancel-in-progress: false

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"

      - run: pip install --quiet pandas requests

      # Deliberately energy-charts, and deliberately not configurable here. This
      # job publishes, and ENTSO-E's day-ahead prices (12.1.d) and scheduled
      # exchanges (12.1.f) are absent from its free-re-use list, so they are not
      # ours to redistribute. energy-charts carries the same prices under CC BY
      # 4.0 from SMARD. ENTSO-E is the right source for local analysis -- see the
      # note at the top of build_data.py before changing this.
      - name: Fetch and merge
        # Inputs arrive as env vars, never interpolated into the script body --
        # `${{ inputs.date }}` inline would be a shell-injection hole.
        env:
          IN_DATE: ${{ inputs.date }}
          IN_END: ${{ inputs.end }}
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          if [ -n "$IN_DATE" ]; then
            if [ -n "$IN_END" ]; then
              python3 build_data.py --date "$IN_DATE" --end "$IN_END"
            else
              python3 build_data.py --date "$IN_DATE"
            fi
          else
            python3 build_data.py \
              --date "$(date -u -d '3 days ago' +%F)" \
              --end  "$(date -u -d 'yesterday' +%F)"
          fi

      - name: Commit if the data moved
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          git config user.name  "github-actions[bot]"
          git config user.email "41898282+github-actions[bot]@users.noreply.github.com"
          git add docs/data/daily.json
          if git diff --staged --quiet; then
            echo "no change"
          else
            git commit -m "data: refresh through $(date -u +%F)"
            git push
          fi

# German cross-border electricity balance

Did Germany pay more for imported electricity than it earned from exports? This
values every cross-border flow at day-ahead prices, per border and per market
time unit, and reports it over a day or a range.

```
de_trade_balance.py    the analysis and CLI report
build_data.py          reshapes a range into docs/data/daily.json
docs/                  the dashboard GitHub Pages serves
```

## Quick start

```bash
pip install pandas requests           # entsoe-py too, for --source entsoe
./de_trade_balance.py --date 2026-08-16          # one day, per MTU
./de_trade_balance.py --date 2026-07             # all of July, per day
./de_trade_balance.py --date 2026 --by week      # the year, per ISO week
./de_trade_balance.py --demo                     # synthetic, no network
```

No account needed: it defaults to Fraunhofer ISE's energy-charts API. Every raw
response is cached under `~/.cache/de_trade_balance`, which matters because that
API is rate limited per IP and endpoint and has no bulk export — a cold month of
all 11 borders costs ~90s and about a dozen requests, then it is free forever.

## The dashboard

```bash
python3 build_data.py --date 2026-07-18 --days 30   # fill the data file
cd docs && python3 -m http.server 8731              # then open localhost:8731
```

`build_data.py` upserts by date, so re-running a day corrects it in place. Both
sources revise the last few days after first publication, which is why the daily
job re-fetches a short trailing window rather than only yesterday.

### Publishing it

Settings → Pages → Source: **Deploy from a branch**, branch `site-daily-dashboard`,
folder **`/docs`**. The data file is committed, so each data commit is a deploy;
there is no build step and no CDN — the page is one HTML file with inline SVG
charts and no dependencies.

`.github/workflows/daily.yml` refreshes the data every morning and commits it.
**GitHub only fires `schedule` on the default branch**, so while this sits on a
side branch the cron will not run — trigger it by hand from the Actions tab
(`workflow_dispatch`, optionally with a date range to backfill), or merge this
branch to make the cron live.

## Which source to use

**ENTSO-E to analyse, energy-charts to publish.** That split is a licensing
decision, not a data-quality one, and it is worth understanding before changing it.

ENTSO-E is the better data: it publishes each direction of a border separately, and
carries DK_2 instead of folding it into DK_1. Use it freely for analysis —
`--source entsoe` with a free token in `ENTSOE_API_TOKEN` and `pip install
entsoe-py`.

But the dashboard *republishes*, and ENTSO-E's
[list of data available for free re-use](https://transparencyplatform.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/40921911218961-Legal-Terms-and-Conditions)
(Article 2.5 of its terms) does not cover the two series this project leans on:

| Series | Article | On the free-re-use list |
|---|---|---|
| Physical flows | 12.1.g | yes, item #18 |
| Day-ahead prices | 12.1.d | **no** |
| Scheduled commercial exchanges | 12.1.f | **no** |

The whole `12.1.d/e/f` market-results block is absent. That is not an oversight:
those series belong to the power exchanges rather than the TSOs, and ENTSO-E cannot
sub-license what it does not hold rights to. The transparency mandate makes the
data *visible*; it does not grant redistribution.

energy-charts carries the same prices for DE-LU and all 11 neighbouring zones under
CC BY 4.0 from Bundesnetzagentur | SMARD.de — a public authority that did license
them openly — which is why the published page uses it. (Its other bidding zones are
marked private/internal use only, so don't widen `NEIGHBOURS` and then publish.)
Checked against the 18 Oct 2023 revision of that list, which does get amended.

Measured over July 2026, the two agree on `balance_at_de_price` to **0.0002%** and
on `congestion_rent` to 0.6% — not luck, but because both reduce to net-only
expressions per MTU:

```
balance_at_de_price = sum(net_MWh * price_de)
congestion_rent     = sum(net_MWh * spread)
```

so a source that reports flows already netted cannot shift either. What it does
shift is everything gross: energy-charts nets opposite flows within a border-hour,
so `import_gwh`/`export_gwh` come out ~26% low, and the volume-weighted prices are
biased apart. It also does not carry DK_2 — though the Kontek energy is still
there, filed under DK_1, so only the zonal pricing suffers.

## Reading the numbers

There is no single true figure, so three are reported. Cross-border trade in the
coupled day-ahead market is *implicit*: nobody buys a labelled MWh from France.
German buyers pay the German price, the seller abroad receives theirs, and the
difference is congestion rent collected by the transmission operators on both
sides — regulated back into grid fees and interconnector investment, not a loss.

Day-ahead only: intraday and balancing trades settle at other prices and are not
included. The long-form version of all of this is the docstring at the top of
`de_trade_balance.py`.

## Attribution

Day-ahead prices for Germany and its neighbours are
[CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/) from
[Bundesnetzagentur | SMARD.de](https://www.smard.de), redistributed unchanged by
[Energy-Charts.info](https://www.energy-charts.info) (Fraunhofer ISE), which is
also the source of the cross-border exchange series. Other bidding zones on that
endpoint are marked private/internal use only — don't widen the border list and
then publish the numbers.

# German cross-border electricity balance

Did Germany pay more for imported electricity than it earned from exports? This
values every cross-border flow at day-ahead prices, per border and per market
time unit, and reports it over a day or a range.

```
de_trade_balance.py    the analysis and CLI report
build_data.py          reshapes a range into docs/data/daily.json
docs/                  the dashboard GitHub Pages serves
```

## Quick start

```bash
pip install pandas requests           # entsoe-py too, for --source entsoe
./de_trade_balance.py --date 2026-08-16          # one day, per MTU
./de_trade_balance.py --date 2026-08-16 --source smard   # gross per-direction flows
./de_trade_balance.py --date 2026-07             # all of July, per day
./de_trade_balance.py --date 2026 --by week      # the year, per ISO week
./de_trade_balance.py --demo                     # synthetic, no network
```

No account needed for either no-auth source. Raw responses are cached under
`~/.cache/de_trade_balance`, which matters most for energy-charts: it is rate
limited per IP and endpoint and has no bulk export, so a cold month of all 11
borders costs ~90s, then is free forever. SMARD is far cheaper — it takes many
series per request, so a month of every border plus prices and load is six
requests in a couple of seconds.

## The dashboard

```bash
python3 build_data.py --date 2026-07-18 --days 30   # fill the data file (SMARD)
cd docs && python3 -m http.server 8731              # then open localhost:8731
```

`build_data.py` upserts by date, so re-running a day corrects it in place. Both
sources revise the last few days after first publication, which is why the daily
job re-fetches a short trailing window rather than only yesterday.

### Publishing it

Settings → Pages → Source: **Deploy from a branch**, branch `site-daily-dashboard`,
folder **`/docs`**. The data file is committed, so each data commit is a deploy;
there is no build step and no CDN — the page is one HTML file with inline SVG
charts and no dependencies.

`.github/workflows/daily.yml` refreshes the data every morning and commits it.
**GitHub only fires `schedule` on the default branch**, so while this sits on a
side branch the cron will not run — trigger it by hand from the Actions tab
(`workflow_dispatch`, optionally with a date range to backfill), or merge this
branch to make the cron live.

## Which source to use

**SMARD** (`--source smard`, the dashboard default). Bundesnetzagentur is the
primary publisher, a public authority, its data is CC BY 4.0, and it carries each
direction of each border separately. It is the only source that is both
publishable and complete — cross-checked against ENTSO-E for 2026-07-18, all 11
borders and both directions, agreeing to under 0.02 GWh. No account needed.

The other two are worth keeping for what they are: **`--source entsoe`** as an
independent cross-check (free token in `ENTSOE_API_TOKEN`, `pip install entsoe-py`),
and **`--source energy-charts`** as a no-fuss fallback with a finer generation-type
taxonomy.

| Source | licence to republish | flows | Denmark |
|---|---|---|---|
| smard | CC BY 4.0, primary publisher | gross per direction | DK_1 / DK_2 split |
| energy-charts | CC BY 4.0 (prices from SMARD) | netted, ~27% low | often unsplit |
| entsoe | prices + scheduled exchanges **not** on the free-re-use list | gross per direction | split |

That last row is the constraint that shapes everything. The dashboard *republishes*,
and ENTSO-E's
[list of data available for free re-use](https://transparencyplatform.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/40921911218961-Legal-Terms-and-Conditions)
(Article 2.5 of its terms) does not cover the two series this project leans on:

| Series | Article | On the free-re-use list |
|---|---|---|
| Physical flows | 12.1.g | yes, item #18 |
| Day-ahead prices | 12.1.d | **no** |
| Scheduled commercial exchanges | 12.1.f | **no** |

The whole `12.1.d/e/f` market-results block is absent. That is not an oversight:
those series belong to the power exchanges rather than the TSOs, and ENTSO-E cannot
sub-license what it does not hold rights to. The transparency mandate makes the
data *visible*; it does not grant redistribution.

SMARD, being the primary publisher and a public authority, licensed the same series
openly — which is why the published page uses it. (energy-charts' non-SMARD bidding
zones are marked private/internal use only, so don't widen `NEIGHBOURS` and then
publish.) Checked against the 18 Oct 2023 revision of that list, which does get
amended.

Measured over July 2026, the two agree on `balance_at_de_price` to **0.0002%** and
on `congestion_rent` to 0.6% — not luck, but because both reduce to net-only
expressions per MTU:

```
balance_at_de_price = sum(net_MWh * price_de)
congestion_rent     = sum(net_MWh * spread)
```

so a source that reports flows already netted cannot shift either. What it does
shift is everything gross: energy-charts nets opposite flows within a border-hour,
so `import_gwh`/`export_gwh` come out ~26% low, and the volume-weighted prices are
biased apart. It also does not carry DK_2 — though the Kontek energy is still
there, filed under DK_1, so only the zonal pricing suffers.

## Reading the numbers

There is no single true figure, so three are reported. Cross-border trade in the
coupled day-ahead market is *implicit*: nobody buys a labelled MWh from France.
German buyers pay the German price, the seller abroad receives theirs, and the
difference is congestion rent collected by the transmission operators on both
sides — regulated back into grid fees and interconnector investment, not a loss.

Day-ahead only: intraday and balancing trades settle at other prices and are not
included. The long-form version of all of this is the docstring at the top of
`de_trade_balance.py`.

Day-ahead prices for Germany and its neighbours are
[CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/) from
[Bundesnetzagentur | SMARD.de](https://www.smard.de), redistributed unchanged by

also the source of the cross-border exchange series. Other bidding zones on that
endpoint are marked private/internal use only — don't widen the border list and
then publish the numbers.

1	#!/usr/bin/env python3
2	"""
3	de_trade_balance.py -- Did Germany pay more for imported electricity than it
4	earned from exports, over a day or over a longer range?
5	
6	Pulls, per border and per market time unit (MTU):
7	  * cross-border exchange DE-LU <-> neighbour, both directions
8	  * day-ahead price of DE-LU and of the neighbouring bidding zone
9	
10	...then values the flows and prints a per-border summary plus a time series at
11	whatever resolution the range warrants (MTU, day, ISO week, month, year).
12	
13	Data source: ENTSO-E Transparency Platform (https://transparency.entsoe.eu).
14	Requires a free API token: register, then Account Settings -> "Generate a new
15	token" (older accounts: email transparency@entsoe.eu asking for API access).
16	
17	    export ENTSOE_API_TOKEN=...             # --source entsoe only
18	    pip install entsoe-py pandas requests
19	    ./de_trade_balance.py --date 2026-08-16                    # one day, per MTU
20	    ./de_trade_balance.py --date 2026-08-16 --source smard     # gross per direction
21	    ./de_trade_balance.py --date 2026-07                       # all of July, per day
22	    ./de_trade_balance.py --date 2026 --by week                # the year, ISO weeks
23	    ./de_trade_balance.py --date 2026-01-01 --end 2026-06-30 --by month
24	    ./de_trade_balance.py --date 2026-08-16 --flows physical --csv out/
25	    ./de_trade_balance.py --demo                               # synthetic data
26	
27	
28	A NOTE ON WHAT "COST" MEANS HERE
29	-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
30	There is no single true number, so this script reports three.
31	
32	In the coupled European day-ahead market, cross-border trade is *implicit*:
33	nobody buys a labelled MWh "from France". Buyers in a zone pay their own zonal
34	price, sellers in a zone receive their own zonal price, and the algorithm moves
35	power across a border until either the prices converge or the interconnector
36	saturates. So for one MWh flowing X -> DE:
37	
38	    German buyers pay          P_DE
39	    the seller in X receives   P_X
40	    the difference (P_DE-P_X)  is congestion rent, collected by the two TSOs
41	                               (normally split 50/50, and regulated back into
42	                               grid fees / interconnector investment)
43	
44	Hence:
45	
46	  balance_at_de_price   Everything valued at the German price. This is the
47	                        "what did this volume trade for at home" view and the
48	                        one journalism usually means. Under this metric, if DE
49	                        is a net importer in expensive hours and a net exporter
50	                        in cheap hours, the balance is negative.
51	
52	                        Worth seeing that it collapses to
53	                        sum(net_MWh * price_de) per MTU: both directions carry
54	                        the same price, so gross volumes cancel and only the
55	                        net position in each hour survives. That makes it the
56	                        sturdiest of the three -- indifferent to whether the
57	                        source reports flows gross or already netted -- and it
58	                        is also why it says nothing about how much trade
59	                        actually took place.
60	
61	  balance_at_zonal      Imports valued at the exporting zone's price, exports
62	                        valued at the German price -- i.e. money actually
63	                        leaving/entering the German market area, ignoring
64	                        congestion rent. Almost always the friendlier number.
65	
66	  congestion_rent       Rent on both legs, which works out as
67	                        sum(net_MWh * spread) per border and MTU: imports earn
68	                        it when P_DE > P_X, exports when P_X > P_DE. Not a loss;
69	                        it is revenue to the two TSOs on that border, normally
70	                        split 50/50.
71	
72	                        It is *not* the gap between the two balances above, easy
73	                        as that is to assume. balance_at_zonal only re-prices
74	                        the import leg -- exports sit at the German price in
75	                        both metrics -- so the gap is the import-side rent
76	                        alone: 43.6 of 99.6 MEUR over July 2026. The export-side
77	                        rent is real TSO revenue that neither balance reports.
78	
79	                        Being net-only per border, it is as indifferent to gross
80	                        volumes as balance_at_de_price. entsoe and energy-charts
81	                        agreed on it to 0.6% for July 2026 despite differing by
82	                        1,499 GWh of gross bidirectional flow; what little gap
83	                        remains is DK_2 finally being priced at its own zone.
84	
85	Also worth keeping in mind:
86	  * Day-ahead is the bulk of it, not all of it. Intraday and balancing trades
87	    are settled at other prices and are not included here.
88	  * "physical" flows (metered, includes loop and transit flows) differ from
89	    "scheduled" commercial exchanges. Only the latter has a price attached in
90	    any meaningful sense, so it is the default. Physical is available for
91	    comparison via --flows physical.

content.text:
Built and committed as `4f77853`. Refresh **http://localhost:8731**.

**SMARD dissolves the trade-off I'd told you was unavoidable.** You now get ENTSO-E's data shape on a licence that permits publishing: gross per-direction flows, DK_2 as a real border, CC BY 4.0 from the primary publisher. Verified against ENTSO-E for 18 July — **all 11 borders, both directions, every one within 0.02 GWh.** The balance moved 0.3 kEUR, being net-only as always.

It's also dramatically cheaper: one POST carries many modules, so a month of every border plus prices and load is **six requests in a couple of seconds**, against ~34 for ENTSO-E and a 90-second rate-limit crawl for energy-charts.

**One bug worth telling you about**, because of how it hid. SMARD returns columns in *its* order, not the order you request modules — but only once a request grows past a handful, which is why my small probes looked fine. Zipping the response to my id list permuted every single border **while leaving the totals exactly correct**. The per-border cross-check against ENTSO-E caught it; a totals check never would have. Columns are now matched by header label, and that's written down in the class.

**The new panel — "What the price had to reach for"** — is a scatter of daily mean price against residual load (demand minus wind and solar), one dot per day, coloured red/blue by whether Germany was a net importer.

A scatter deliberately: those are different measures, and putting GW and €/MWh on a shared time axis would need two y-scales — the one chart form that reliably manufactures a correlation that isn't there. Here each measure owns an axis and the relationship *is* the reading.

It answers what your balance chart structurally cannot: **the price tracks how far into the dispatchable stack the day had to reach (r = 0.79), and the days Germany imported are the days it reached furthest.** Blue dots cluster low-left, red high-right. That's the mechanism from our market-coupling conversation, visible in one panel. Residual load and load also joined the table view and the tooltips.

Verified in both themes at 1280px and 390px, no console errors, no overflow, filters and tooltips exercised. That caught a second bug: the new card was being drawn while still `hidden`, so it measured 0 wide, the fallback width took over, and the SVG scaled down — shrinking every label. Only visible on mobile, where legibility matters most.

Two notes:

- **The daily workflow needs no secret now.** It uses SMARD, no token, and deliberately takes no source input — the licence reasoning is in a comment at the fetch step so nobody switches it casually.
- **`--source entsoe` is now the cross-check**, and it earned that role twice today: it caught the column permutation, and it validated the gross volumes. Worth keeping the token around for exactly that.

Reworked and committed (`3b2245c`) — refresh and have another look.

You were right that it wasn't working. The chart was *asserting* its finding (an `r = 0.79` in the caption) rather than showing it, and a chart that needs its paragraph to be understood is doing the wrong job. Four changes:

- **The trend line is now drawn** — least-squares, clipped to the plot rectangle so a steep slope can't poke out of the top corner. The relationship is a line you can see instead of a number you have to trust.
- **The x axis says which way it runs**: `← more wind & sun` on the left, `less wind & sun →` on the right. "Residual load" gave you a quantity with no direction to hold in your head; now the axis tells you what moving right *means*.
- **The extremes are labelled** — 18 Jul (most wind and sun) and 31 Jul (least) — so the cloud has two landmarks instead of being thirty anonymous dots.
- **The title states the finding**: "Cheap days are windy days", rather than the riddle "What the price had to reach for". The caption now opens with how to read a single dot.

The read should be, without help: dots climb left to right along the grey line; the left end is blue and cheap, the right end is red and dear. Wind and sun scarce → power dear → Germany imports.

Also fixed a genuine bug your comment led me to: at 390px the three axis labels overlapped into an unreadable smear. They now only share the axis line when there's room, and the title drops to a second line otherwise.

**If it still doesn't land, the honest alternative is a different form.** Every other panel on the page is a daily time series, and this is the only scatter — that inconsistency may be the real cost. I could instead show residual load as daily columns directly beneath the price chart, sharing the same date axis, so you'd read it by seeing the two shapes rise and fall together. That's more familiar and more consistent with the page, though it shows co-movement rather than the relationship itself, and you'd be comparing two panels by eye instead of reading one.
